# Configuration — all fields of `TinySesamConfig`

<!-- GENERATED by scripts/_config_docs.py — do not maintain by hand.
     Rebuild: `python3 scripts/_config_docs.py` -->

The source is `tinysesam/config.py`; this page is its extract. What a field *means* is written
there as a comment — here in the same order, grouped by topic.

The READMEs explain the **paths** (which method for what, how to combine them). This
reference answers the other question: *"There is a field — what does it do?"*

Presets (`TinySesamConfig.local_accounts()`, `.oidc_gateway()`, …) set bundles of these fields;
individual ones can be overridden via `**overrides`.

**Tier:** Every field belongs to tier A — public, stable from 1.0 (see [API.md](API.md), “Three tiers”), except `totp_required` (B).

## Branding/theme: set once → re-skins ALL built-in pages (+ error pages)

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `brand_css` | `str` | `""` | additional CSS (after the default → overrides it) |
| `brand_head` | `str` | `""` | additional <head> HTML (e.g. logo font, meta) |
| `brand_icon` | `str` | `""` | favicon URL for ALL built-in pages (empty = built-in default icon, "none" = none; since 0.24.8 — before, empty meant "none") |
| `brand_backgrounds` | `list` | `list` | Background images of all built-in pages (since 0.24.8): paths, data: or https addresses. Several fade slowly into one another, with a very dark overlay on top; with "reduce motion" the first one stays still. An https address opens the strict CSP for exactly that origin (img-src). Loading images from third parties means: every visitor's browser contacts them — only on purpose and with a suitable licence. |
| `brand_background_seconds` | `int` | `12` | how long each image stays before the cross-fade |
| `brand_background_credit_text` | `str` | `""` | discreet note at the bottom right, e.g. "Photos: Unsplash" |
| `brand_background_credit_url` | `str` | `""` | target of the note (http/https only) |
| `brand_header` | `object` | `""` | Shell of the host app around EVERY built-in page (login/PIN/TOTP/account/admin/error): your own navigation on top, footer at the bottom. Either an HTML string or `fn(auth) -> str` if the content depends on the request (login state, language) — then evaluated on every call. |
| `brand_footer` | `object` | `""` | footer below every built-in page; HTML string or `fn(auth) -> str` |

## Roles/groups

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `admin_implies_roles` | `bool` | `True` | Does an admin satisfy EVERY require_role(...) check? Default True (classic behaviour). CAUTION: if an app's permissions hang solely on an IdP group, this is a silent privilege escalation — set False then, or use `require_role(..., admin_implies=False)` per guard. |
| `group_match` | `str` | `"exact"` | How are IdP groups compared with the keys of *_group_role_map? "exact" (default, safe) or "substring" (the old substring comparison, on request only). With "exact", LDAP compares a memberOf DN by its parts: the whole DN, "cn=staff" or "staff". |
| `available_roles` | `list[str]` | `list` | Known roles/groups: the admin panel offers them as checkboxes (empty = free-text fallback). |
| `oidc_group_role_map` | `dict` | `dict` | IdP group → local role (set on OIDC/SAML/LDAP login). Target "__admin__" = admin flag (grant only). Compared according to `group_match` (default exact). Managed roles are synchronised on each login. |
| `saml_group_role_map` | `dict` | `dict` | SAML group → local role, e.g. `{"staff": "editors"}` |
| `ldap_group_role_map` | `dict` | `dict` | LDAP group (DN or name) → local role |

## Active login methods (all can run in parallel)

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `password_enabled` | `bool` | `True` | offer password login at all (off = SSO/passkey/PIN only) |
| `password_blocklist_file` | `str` | `""` | Own blocklist for new passwords: path to a text file, one password per line (UTF-8, lines in another encoding count as Latin-1; `#` at the start of a line = comment). Complements the small built-in list — if you want to check against the common leak lists (e.g. the 100,000 most frequent), put them here. Offline: TinySesam asks no third-party service. Empty = built-in list only. `tinysesam passwd` reads it with `--blocklist-file`. |
| `passkey_enabled` | `bool` | `False` | WebAuthn / passkeys (passwordless) — needs [passkey] |
| `passkey_user_verification` | `str` | `"required"` | Must the authenticator verify the human (PIN, fingerprint, face) before it signs? `"required"` (default) demands it, `"preferred"` asks for it and also accepts a no (B2-10). Why it matters: A passkey signs in **on its own** in TinySesam — it is not a second factor but a complete login. Without user verification it only proves **possession** of the key: the unlocked computer, the plugged-in stick, the phone briefly put down are enough then. With it, it proves possession **and** something only the person can do. Up to 0.18.x this was "preferred" and the answer was not even checked — an authenticator could say no and still count. `"preferred"` is a deliberate decision for a stock of old authenticators and announces itself at startup. Whoever starts fresh leaves it at `"required"`. |
| `pin_enabled` | `bool` | `False` | personal PIN per user (username + PIN) |
| `pin_login` | `bool` | `True` | offer the PIN as first factor on the login page. False = the PIN exists but serves ONLY as an additional factor (chain step, route chain) or as step-up for sensitive areas. If a strict login_chain demands the PIN behind another factor, it is never a first factor there. |
| `pin_min_length` | `int` | `4` | minimum length when setting a PIN |
| `stepup_methods` | `list[str]` | `list` | What confirms a step-up (require(mfa=True))? Empty = everything the user has set up (order totp → pin → password). E.g. ["pin"] = PIN for sensitive areas. If the user has none of the listed methods, their best available method applies. |
| `stepup_strict` | `bool` | `False` | Turn the wish into a barrier: True = whoever has none of the listed methods set up does NOT get in (instead of confirming with the password they just signed in with — that is no step-up). Default False, because otherwise the area would be locked for existing accounts overnight; whoever sets `stepup_methods` to enforce something usually wants True as well. |
| `oidc_enabled` | `bool` | `False` | external IdProvider (PocketID …) |
| `oidc_callback_path` | `str` | `"/auth/oidc/callback"` | Path of the callback. Must be registered with the IdP as redirect URI (base_url + this path). At startup TinySesam logs the expected URI — otherwise typos only show up after the login. |
| `apikey_enabled` | `bool` | `True` | access via API key (machines/daemons, bound to a user/service account) |
| `apikey_default_days` | `int` | `90` | Lifetime of an automation key in days if the caller names none. A key without expiry is a secret nobody takes back: it outlives the person who issued it, the project it was meant for, and the machine it sits on. |
| `apikey_allow_unlimited` | `bool` | `False` | May an automation key be created without expiry (`expires_days=0`)? Default no. True is a deliberate decision of the operator and is logged on creation — there are cases for it (a device nobody can touch), they are just rare. |
| `admin_enabled` | `bool` | `True` | mount the admin panel automatically at admin_path |
| `admin_path` | `str` | `"/auth/admin"` | default mount point; auth.admin_router() also lets you mount it elsewhere |
| `admin_ui_enabled` | `bool` | `True` | built-in HTML UI; False = JSON API only (for embedding in your own panel) |
| `account_enabled` | `bool` | `True` | built-in self-service page /auth/account (overridable) |
| `forward_auth_enabled` | `bool` | `False` | /auth/forward + /auth/verify for reverse proxy (Caddy/nginx/Traefik) |
| `forward_headers` | `dict` | `dict` | Which headers the forward-auth response sets. Empty = the Authelia-style set Remote-User/-Name/-Email/-Groups and Remote-Id (the account ID — stable across renames and mail changes, since 2026-09-25). Otherwise **field → header name** (or list of names); what is not listed here is NOT set. Fields: user · name · email · groups · id. The proxy must set EVERY configured header itself (overwrite) — otherwise it passes on one of the same name sent by the browser (deploy/forward-auth/*). {"user": "X-WEBAUTH-USER"}                     → Grafana style, and nothing else {"user": ["Remote-User", "X-Auth-Request-User"], "groups": "X-Auth-Request-Groups"} With the Traefik/Caddy example, keep the forwarded headers in sync (authResponseHeaders). |
| `gate_token_enabled` | `bool` | `False` | Gate token (ADR-9, T-19): A successful forward-auth check additionally returns a short-lived, signed token (Ed25519) in the header X-TinySesam-Gate-Cookie. The proxy sets it as a cookie on the application's host and verifies it itself from then on (Caddy + caddy-jwt) — TinySesam is only asked again when it is missing or expired. Only with forward_auth_enabled, only for sessions (not for API keys) and only for hosts from trusted_redirect_hosts or oidc_clients. Template: deploy/forward-auth/Caddyfile.gate. |
| `gate_token_ttl_sec` | `int` | `300` | lifetime = revocation delay at the proxy; 30–3600 |
| `forward_login` | `str` | `"page"` | How the gate signs in someone who is not signed in (T-21): "page" = TinySesam's login page (with the application's name from forward_apps), "direct" = on page load straight to the identity provider and back to the requested address. "direct" only if OIDC is the only sign-in method; background requests (XHR, assets) go to the login page even then — otherwise each of them would start a flow of its own. oidc_gateway() sets "direct". |
| `forward_logout` | `str` | `"all"` | What "sign out" means at the application (T-22), path: https://<app>/.tinysesam/logout. "all" = end this session (applies to all applications behind the same sign-in) and, with oidc_rp_logout, at the provider too; "app" = this application only: the session stays, the host lets it through again only after "Continue as …" on the login page; "ask" = ask. |
| `forward_logged_out_sec` | `int` | `10` | "Signed out" page in "direct" mode (PO 2026-10-10): leave it up for this many seconds, then go back to the application on its own — the gate forwards to the provider, where a NEW sign-in begins (the provider is already signed out with oidc_rp_logout). 0 = leave it up, button only. 0–300. |
| `forward_apps` | `dict` | `dict` | Settings per protected application: {"app.example.com": {"name": "Wiki", "login": "direct", "logout": "ask"}}. name = display name on the login and sign-out pages; login/logout override forward_login/forward_logout for this host. |
| `gate_cookie_name` | `str` | `"__Host-tinysesam_gate"` | form __Host-tinysesam_<name>: host-only, and the templates strip it before the app |
| `gate_link_enabled` | `bool` | `False` | Central gateway, session stays on its host (T-26): An app host gets, via a code exchange (/.tinysesam/start → /auth/gate/authorize → /.tinysesam/callback), only a connection cookie of its own that is valid for it alone. Without this, the session cookie would have to sit on the parent domain and would reach every app below it. Requires gate_token_enabled and base_url, does not combine with cookie_domain. |
| `https_mode` | `str` | `"warn"` | off \| warn \| force  — force = HTTP→HTTPS redirect; warn = also runs WITHOUT a certificate (with a warning in the panel) |
| `login_identifier` | `str` | `"both"` | What do people sign in with? "username" \| "email" \| "both" (both allowed in the same field) |

| `admin_identifiers` | `list[str]` | `list` | username/email promoted to admin at login AS LONG AS there is no admin — and never again after the identity provider of the instance has revoked its last admin (G6; then one-time token or `tinysesam owner`). Also works with OIDC/SAML/LDAP (usually the email there). |

## Magic link (one-time login/access by email)

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `magiclink_enabled` | `bool` | `False` | sign-in by one-time link — needs a mailer |
| `magiclink_ttl_min` | `int` | `15` | validity of a one-time link |
| `magiclink_require_second_factor` | `bool` | `True` | ASVS 6.3.6 (PO decision 2026-09-24): If an account has a second factor (TOTP or passkey), the sign-in link alone does not sign in fully — the factor is demanded afterwards. Otherwise the mailbox would be the only key, even for an account that protected itself with an authenticator. Accounts without a second factor are still signed in by the link alone. Applies to the global chain and every route chain (`require(factors=["magic"])`, G10). `False` = the link always suffices (behaviour up to 0.20.x in chains like `["magic"]`). |

## Self-service: address and username (PO decision 2026-09-25)

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `self_service_email_change` | `bool` | `True` | Everyone changes their own email address (account page, fresh step-up). The new one counts only after the click on the confirmation link sent to it; the old one gets a notice. Needs a mailer — without one this path does not exist. |
| `self_service_username_change` | `bool` | `True` | Everyone changes their own username (account page, fresh step-up) — not in the mode `login_identifier="email"`, where the name follows the address, and not alongside LDAP (`ldap_enabled`), where the names come from the directory and only the operator renames. Apps behind forward auth then see a different `Remote-User`; `Remote-Id` is stable. |
| `email_change_ttl_min` | `int` | `60` | validity of the confirmation link for a new address |

## TOTP (2FA on top of password/OIDC; passkeys are already phishing-resistant)

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `totp_enabled` | `bool` | `True` | users may set up TOTP |
| `secrets_key_file` | `str` | `""` | Key file for encrypting the TOTP secrets (H-14/H-15; 32 bytes, Base64). The environment variable TINYSESAM_SECRETS_KEY takes precedence; with neither, TinySesam creates `<db_path>.key` (0600). Without the key all TOTP setups are lost — back it up separately from the database (docs/OPERATIONS.md). |
| `totp_required` | `bool` | `False` | **Tier B.** CAUTION: ineffective and therefore REJECTED since 0.18.0 — the switch was never read. Making TOTP mandatory works through the factor chain: login_chain=['password', 'totp']  (+ login_chain_strict=True) The field only stays so that an existing call gets a clear error instead of a TypeError about an unknown argument. |
| `recovery_code_count` | `int` | `10` | number of one-time recovery codes per generation (lost authenticator) |

## Factor chains (ordered combinations)

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `login_chain` | `list[str]` | `list` | Global default chain of satisfied factors that make a session complete, e.g. ["oidc", "password"] or ["password", "totp"]. Empty = classic (one first factor + TOTP if set up). Can be tightened per route: Depends(auth.require(factors=[...], strict=...)) — in addition, never instead of this chain (since 2026-09-27). Factor names: password, pin, oidc, passkey, totp, magic. The first factor identifies the user. |
| `mfa_enrollment` | `str` | `"first_login"` | Who may set up a second factor demanded by the chain **themselves**? (R3-1) `login_chain=["password", "totp"]` reads like "nobody gets in without a second factor". Up to 0.18.x that was not true: An account without TOTP could set it up at exactly this point itself — so whoever had only the password bound their own authenticator and was fully in. The chain thus protected everyone except those it was meant for. * ``"first_login"`` (default): allowed as long as the account has **never** been fully signed in. A freshly created account sets itself up the first time — never again afterwards. Without a deadline: Whoever uses their new account only in three weeks should not stand in front of a locked door. * ``"grace"``: allowed within `mfa_enrollment_grace_days` after account creation. * ``"strict"``: never. The setup then comes from the operator (`auth.grant_mfa_enrollment(uid)`, admin panel or invitation). If the chain demands no second factor at all, none of this applies — a voluntary TOTP can be set up by any signed-in user at any time, as before. |
| `mfa_enrollment_grace_days` | `int` | `7` | Only for `mfa_enrollment="grace"`: days since account creation. |
| `login_chain_strict` | `bool` | `True` | enforce the order (True) or any order (False) |

## Sessions (server-side, revocable)

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `session_cookie` | `str` | `"tinysesam_session"` | name of the session cookie (tell them apart when several apps share a domain) |
| `session_ttl_hours` | `int` | `24 * 7` | TTL with "stay signed in" (persistent cookie) |
| `session_ttl_transient_hours` | `int` | `12` | TTL without "stay signed in" (session cookie, ends when the browser closes) |
| `remember_me_enabled` | `bool` | `True` | offer the "stay signed in" checkbox (off → always persistent) |
| `session_idle_minutes` | `int` | `8 * 60` | inactivity without "stay signed in" (minutes, 0 = off) |
| `session_idle_minutes_remember` | `int` | `0` | inactivity WITH "stay signed in" (minutes, 0 = off) |
| `session_rotation_grace_sec` | `int` | `10` | Grace period after rotating the token (A-6, PO decision 2026-09-25): A step-up gives the session a new token (F-06). A request that was already in flight at that moment (second tab, background loading) still carries the old one and failed once. For this many seconds the old token keeps working — without step-up freshness, and it ends with the new session. 0 = off. |
| `cookie_secure` | `bool` | `True` | send over HTTPS only |
| `cookie_samesite` | `str` | `"lax"` | lax\|strict\|none |
| `cookie_path` | `str` | `"/"` | path the cookies apply to |
| `cookie_domain` | `str` | `""` | Empty = host-only. For SSO across subdomains e.g. ".example.com" — then TinySesam trusts every host under this domain: Anyone can set a session cookie for the whole domain and so push the browser into someone else's account (known limitation, SECURITY.md). Empty protects against that only as long as the session cookie carries `__Host-` (`cookie_host_prefix`). |
| `cookie_host_prefix` | `bool` | `True` | `__Host-` prefix for session, CSRF and unlock cookie (H-1). Only takes effect where the browser allows it: `cookie_secure=True`, `cookie_domain` empty, `cookie_path="/"`. The CSRF cookie is always host-only and carries the prefix even with `cookie_domain` set. A cookie named like this cannot be set or shadowed by a neighbouring subdomain (cookie tossing). If the prefix is missing on the session cookie (`cookie_domain` set, this switch off, `cookie_path` ≠ "/" or `cookie_secure=False`), it carries only its bare name (`tinysesam_session`), and every host under the domain can plant one (known limitation, SECURITY.md). The cookie name changes with this — sign in once more after the update; the cookies under the old names are deleted by TinySesam on the next sign-in, step-up or sign-out via the built-in routes, `auth.logout()` or `auth.rotate_session()`. Your own code takes the name from `auth.csrf_cookie_name`, not from `csrf_cookie`; your own JS gets it from the page (template variable or `<meta>`) or reads the token from the form field that `auth.ensure_csrf()` returns. |
| `cookie_prefix` | `str` | `"tinysesam_"` | Prefix of THIS installation's cookies (session, CSRF, unlock, OIDC/SAML/passkey flow): Every name that starts with `tinysesam_` then starts with this prefix. For an app with its own TinySesam BEHIND a TinySesam gateway: Its proxy templates strip every `tinysesam_*` cookie before the app — including its OIDC flow cookie, and the way back from the provider failed ("without matching flow cookie"). With e.g. `"myapp_"` its cookies get through. A gateway itself (`forward_auth_enabled`) stays at `tinysesam_`: otherwise the templates no longer strip its session (the config check reports this). Explicitly set names (`session_cookie="x"`) stay as they are; so do the gateway's cookies (`__Host-tinysesam_gate` etc.). Changing it = new cookie names: sign in once more. |

## Content Security Policy for the OWN pages (login/account/TOTP/…)

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `csp` | `str` | `"strict"` | The built-in pages are built nonce-proof (no inline handler, no style=); a nonce is generated per response and injected into every <script>/<style>. "strict" (default) → default-src 'self'; script-src/style-src by nonce only "off"              → no CSP header (e.g. if a proxy/an app sets the CSP centrally) custom string      → used 1:1 as the header; a contained {nonce} is replaced. Without a single known directive ('Strict', 'stirct') the setup aborts instead of silently switching the CSP off; an unknown one next to known ones ('scirpt-src', 'require-sri-for') gives a warning Applies to the pages rendered by TinySesam and the admin panel, not to your own response overrides (they set their CSP themselves). With 'strict', X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN is added; nosniff, Referrer-Policy, no-store and Vary: Cookie are carried by all TinySesam responses regardless of this switch. |

## CSRF (double-submit cookie; in addition to SameSite=Lax)

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `csrf_enabled` | `bool` | `True` | state-changing POSTs demand a token (form field _csrf / header X-CSRF-Token) |
| `csrf_cookie` | `str` | `"tinysesam_csrf"` | name of the CSRF cookie |
| `csrf_origin_check` | `bool` | `True` | Check the origin before the token comparison (H-2): `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` suffices, otherwise `Origin` must be one of our own hosts (Host header, X-Forwarded-Host, base_url — NOT trusted_redirect_hosts: those are redirect targets, in the forward-auth setup the protected apps); `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site` or `cross-site` without an own origin (also `Origin: null`) is rejected. If no usable origin exists and `Sec-Fetch-Site` says `none` or is missing, the token alone decides. `Sec-Fetch-Site` is missing not only with old browsers and scripts but with every browser over HTTP (except localhost): Browsers send `Sec-Fetch-*` to HTTPS only. With `cookie_secure=False` an `Origin: null` from a neighbouring subdomain therefore also gets through to the token, and the CSRF cookie carries no `__Host-` then — over HTTP the check does not protect against login CSRF from the neighbourhood (there the session cookie can be planted anyway, known limitation in SECURITY.md). Behind a proxy that rewrites the host without setting X-Forwarded-Host, browsers without `Sec-Fetch-Site` fail (Safari before 16.4, every browser over HTTP) — set base_url for that. |

## LDAP / lldap (password against directory bind; counts as factor 'password')

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `federation_require_stable_id` | `bool` | `False` | Must a foreign identity (LDAP, SAML) bring a stable identifier? Default **no**: A directory that provides none should not suddenly sign in nobody after the update. If it is missing, the mapping falls back to the username — the unprotected state from before 0.20.0 — and says so once per source in the security log. True turns this into a rejection; that is the safe setting as soon as the directory can. |
| `federation_name_binding_days` | `int` | `30` | How long may a sign-in via LDAP/SAML bind a still unbound account by its **name** (days)? Counted per source from the first start with the source enabled (for existing data: from the update) or from the account's creation, whichever is later. After that the name no longer binds — otherwise a dormant account (someone has left) would fall to the next person who gets the same name in the directory, along with roles and admin rights (G1). Rejection comes with a log line naming the identifier and the remedy; the operator then binds explicitly: `auth.federation_bind_existing(source)` (existing data, dry run as default) or `auth.federation_unbind(source, user_id)` (opens the binding for this account). `0` = explicit only (even a freshly created pre-provisioned account does not bind itself), `-1` = unlimited, the behaviour up to 0.20.x (the config check warns). |
| `ldap_enabled` | `bool` | `False` | check passwords against an LDAP/AD instead of locally — needs [ldap] |
| `ldap_url` | `str` | `""` | ldap://host:389 or ldaps://host:636 |
| `ldap_start_tls` | `bool` | `False` | upgrade to TLS after connecting (port 389); for 636 use `ldaps://` in the URL |
| `ldap_tls_verify` | `bool` | `True` | Verify the directory's certificate? Default **yes** (F-12). Without verification, encrypted only means "not readable by someone who is not in between": Whoever redirects the traffic presents a certificate of their own, gets the password of the service account and of every user password, and passes the response on — nobody notices. Until 0.19.0 the verification did not exist at all. |
| `ldap_tls_ca_file` | `str` | `""` | Own CA file (PEM) for the directory certificate. Empty = the system store. The usual way for an internal directory with its own CA. |
| `ldap_allow_plaintext` | `bool` | `False` | May the connection use no TLS at all (`ldap://` without StartTLS)? Default **no**. Then the password of the service account and every user password would cross the network in clear text. True is a deliberate decision for a directory on the same host (loopback) and announces itself at startup. |
| `ldap_user_dn_template` | `str` | `""` | direct bind, e.g. "uid={username},ou=people,dc=example,dc=com" (lldap) |
| `ldap_bind_dn` | `str` | `""` | OR service account for search-then-bind |
| `ldap_bind_password` | `str` | `""` | password of the service account — belongs in an environment variable |
| `ldap_user_base` | `str` | `""` | search base (for search-then-bind) |
| `ldap_user_filter` | `str` | `"(uid={username})"` | search filter for the account; `{username}` is substituted |
| `ldap_attr_id` | `str` | `""` | The attribute with the directory entry's **stable** identifier (F-11). Empty = try `entryUUID` (OpenLDAP, lldap) and `objectGUID` (Active Directory) in that order. The mapping to the local account hangs on it — a username is no good for that: Whoever renames in the directory or recreates a deleted account under the same name would otherwise get the same local account along with its roles. |
| `ldap_attr_email` | `str` | `"mail"` | LDAP attribute with the email address |
| `ldap_email_trusted` | `bool` | `False` | Trust addresses from the directory across the board? LDAP delivers no proof like OIDC `email_verified`. `False` (default since PO decision 2026-09-25): The address is not used directly — with `federation_email_confirm` the owner confirms it by link, or `ldap_attr_email_verified` names a proof. `True`: The directory is maintained, nobody changes their own `mail` attribute — the address counts as proven and carries rights (first admin via `admin_identifiers`). |
| `ldap_attr_email_verified` | `str` | `""` | LDAP attribute whose true value ("TRUE", "1", "yes") proves THIS entry's address — for directories that keep it. Empty = none. |
| `ldap_attr_name` | `str` | `"cn"` | LDAP attribute with the display name |
| `ldap_group_attr` | `str` | `"memberOf"` | attribute with the group membership |
| `ldap_allowed_groups` | `list[str]` | `list` | empty = all; otherwise gate (DN, "cn=x" or "x" — no substring) |
| `ldap_auto_create` | `bool` | `True` | create an unknown LDAP user locally (without a local password) |

## OIDC

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `oidc_name` | `str` | `"SSO"` | display name of the button |
| `oidc_issuer` | `str` | `""` | e.g. https://id.example.com  (…/.well-known/openid-configuration) |
| `oidc_client_id` | `str` | `""` | client ID at the provider |
| `oidc_client_secret` | `str` | `""` | client secret — belongs in an environment variable, not in the source code |
| `oidc_scopes` | `str` | `"openid profile email"` | requested scopes; `openid` is mandatory, `email`/`profile` fill the account |
| `oidc_auto_create` | `bool` | `True` | create an unknown OIDC user automatically |
| `oidc_email_verified_default` | `bool` | `False` | What applies if the provider does NOT send `email_verified`? The claim is optional in OIDC Core 5.1 (Entra ID, for one, omits it). Default False = the address counts as unconfirmed: It is taken into the account as usual and passed on (`Remote-Email`), but carries no rights — first admin via `admin_identifiers` demands the proof (recorded as `users.email_verified=0`, then applies to EVERY sign-in method of this account). True only for IdPs that do not send the claim AND whose addresses the operator vouches for themselves (own directory, one tenant): then an address without the claim counts as proven and can carry the first admin. A claim that explicitly says `false` stays a no in both cases. |
| `oidc_rp_logout` | `bool` | `False` | on sign-out also sign out of the OIDC provider (end_session), optional |
| `oidc_group_claim` | `str` | `"groups"` | claim with the groups |
| `oidc_allowed_groups` | `list[str]` | `list` | empty = all allowed |

## Several applications behind ONE installation (T-14)

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `oidc_clients` | `dict` | `dict` | Protected host → own OIDC client at the same provider. Empty = one application, the single client above applies to everything (behaviour up to 0.18.0, unchanged). Why at all: Who may enter which application is decided by the **provider** — with PocketID through the group approval per OIDC client. This approval hangs on the client, not on the user. With a single client there is therefore only one answer for all applications: Whoever is in at one is in at all. The previous remedy was a TinySesam instance of its own per application — three containers, three databases, three audit logs for the same people. Structure per entry: ``{"app.example.com": {"client_id": "...", "client_secret": "...", "scopes": "openid profile email", "allowed_groups": [...], "group_role_map": {...}}}``. If an optional key is missing, the single client's value applies. The **issuer is the same for all clients** — several providers in one instance are not intended, and the config check says so too. |
| `oidc_revalidate_minutes` | `int` | `0` | After how many minutes an approval already granted is re-checked at the provider. 0 = never (behaviour up to 0.18.0). The provider decides on the approval, so a revocation must arrive there too: Without re-checking it applies until the session ends — by default seven days. The re-check is a hop via the provider; its session normally persists, so the human sees only a short redirect. If the provider refuses, the approval is gone **for this one application**, the session stays for the others. ``oidc_gateway()`` sets 60; whoever builds it by hand decides for themselves. Allowed are 0 to 43200 (30 days) — above that it is no longer a re-check. A period of one day or more written in seconds is therefore an error; above one day (1440) the check warns and asks for the unit (3600 for an hour). Shorter periods in seconds (300 instead of 5) go unnoticed — the unit is in the field name. |
| `oidc_session_refresh_minutes` | `int` | `15` | Revocation follows the provider (4a): Every so many minutes, on the next request, TinySesam exchanges the refresh token of the OIDC session. If the provider refuses (blocked, deleted, revoked for the application), the session ends; groups and the admin flag granted by the provider are re-evaluated in the process. An unreachable provider signs nobody out. Needs a provider that issues refresh tokens (if necessary scope `offline_access`). 0 = off. |
| `oidc_session_max_unverified_hours` | `int` | `25` | Upper limit without a successful re-check (PO decision 2026-09-25): If 4a fails permanently because of a client error (secret renewed at the provider, client deleted) or the provider itself, nobody re-checks any more — whoever is blocked at the provider in the meantime would stay signed in until the session expires. After this many hours without a yes the session ends; the next sign-in then shows whether the way to the provider works again. Price: If the provider is gone for longer, all OIDC sessions are signed out afterwards. 0 = no limit. |
| `oidc_apikey_confirm_days` | `int` | `30` | API keys of an OIDC account follow the provider (finding 8). If it says no on the re-check (4a), the account's keys go dormant immediately — fixed, cannot be switched off. In addition they apply only as long as the provider has confirmed the account within the last so many days (login via it or a refresh exchange with yes): Whoever works by script only has no session that 4a could re-check. Nothing is deleted — the next sign-in via the provider wakes the keys up again. Accounts without an OIDC binding (including service accounts) are not affected. 0 = no deadline (only the no counts). |

## SAML 2.0 (SP login against an IdP: ADFS, Keycloak, Okta, Entra …)

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `saml_enabled` | `bool` | `False` | SAML 2.0 sign-in against an IdP — needs [saml] and libxmlsec1 |
| `saml_name` | `str` | `"SAML"` | display name of the button |
| `saml_sp_entity_id` | `str` | `""` | own SP entity ID; empty = base_url + /auth/saml/metadata |
| `saml_acs_url` | `str` | `""` | Assertion Consumer Service; empty = base_url + /auth/saml/acs |
| `saml_idp_entity_id` | `str` | `""` | IdP entity ID. Empty = the SSO URL is assumed — that is right for some IdPs, for others it is NOT: Keycloak, for example, calls itself `https://…/realms/<realm>`, while the SSO URL ends in `/protocol/saml`. If it does not match, every assertion is rejected ("Invalid issuer"); the reason is then in the logger `tinysesam.security`. When in doubt, copy it from the IdP descriptor (`entityID=` in the metadata XML). |
| `saml_idp_sso_url` | `str` | `""` | IdP single-sign-on URL (redirect binding) |
| `saml_idp_x509cert` | `str` | `""` | IdP signing certificate (PEM body, without BEGIN/END) |
| `saml_attr_username` | `str` | `""` | attribute with the username; empty = NameID |
| `saml_attr_email` | `str` | `"email"` | SAML attribute with the email address |
| `saml_email_trusted` | `bool` | `False` | Trust addresses from the assertion across the board? SAML has no proof. `False` (default): The address is not used directly — no account attribute, no `Remote-Email`, an account name with `@` yields to a substitute name (like H-3 for OIDC); with `federation_email_confirm` the owner confirms it by link, or `saml_attr_email_verified` names a proof. `True`: The IdP verifies every address (corporate IdP without self-registration). |
| `saml_attr_email_verified` | `str` | `""` | Attribute of the assertion whose true value proves the address (e.g. a Keycloak mapper for `emailVerified`). Empty = none. |
| `federation_email_confirm` | `bool` | `True` | Have addresses from LDAP/SAML that are not trusted confirmed by link (PO decision 2026-09-25): After sign-in a confirmation link goes to the address from the source — at most one delivered per account and day (across all workers; if a link lives longer, `email_change_ttl_min`, that long), none while one is open; a throttle or a failed delivery is retried after `mail_per_address_window_sec`. An address already taken or reserved gets none, its rejection counts like a delivery. Only the click makes it the account's address, with proof. Needs mailer and `base_url`. |
| `saml_attr_name` | `str` | `"displayName"` | SAML attribute with the display name |
| `saml_attr_id` | `str` | `""` | The attribute with the **stable** identifier (F-11). Empty = the assertion's `NameID`. It is only suitable if its format is permanent: `persistent` or an own identifier from the directory. A **transient** NameID format changes with every sign-in and is worthless as a binding — then an attribute the IdP reliably sends belongs here. |
| `saml_attr_groups` | `str` | `"groups"` | SAML attribute with the groups (for saml_group_role_map) |
| `saml_allowed_groups` | `list[str]` | `list` | empty = all |
| `saml_auto_create` | `bool` | `True` | create unknown users on their first successful SAML login |

## App integration

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `base_url` | `str` | `""` | Public base URL — the one address under which the app is reachable from outside. Source for EVERY absolute address: links in mails (reset, magic, confirmation, invitation), OIDC redirect URI and post-logout, SAML entity ID/ACS, forward-auth redirect. MANDATORY as soon as a mail path (magiclink_enabled, password_reset_enabled, signup_verify_email), oidc_enabled or saml_enabled is on — otherwise the setup fails with ConfigError. Reason: The Host header would remain as the source, and that is input from the requester; without base_url an attacker could redirect the reset link in the victim's mail to their own server. trusted_redirect_hosts is no substitute for it — if more than one host is listed there, the requester chooses via the Host header. If mounted under a subpath (root_path), the prefix belongs HERE: "https://example.com/sso" — it applies to the LINKS SENT OUT, which carry it exactly once. The built-in pages and their redirects take the same prefix since T-15 from the path of this base_url (without base_url from the request's root_path). login_path, login_redirect, logout_redirect and admin_path are therefore paths of the app WITHOUT the prefix. Where base_url may stay empty (password/passkey/PIN/LDAP only, forward_auth_enabled at most), a derived base is checked: only a host from trusted_redirect_hosts or loopback counts, and the server's root_path comes along. If base_url is set, it ALWAYS wins — even against a base passed in from outside on a second own host from trusted_redirect_hosts (otherwise the Host header chooses which of our own names ends up in the reset link). |
| `login_path` | `str` | `"/auth/login"` | login page |
| `login_redirect` | `str` | `"/"` | target after a successful login |
| `logout_redirect` | `str` | `"/auth/login"` | target after logout |

## Hardening

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trusted_proxies` | `list[str]` | `["127.0.0.1/32", "::1/128"]` | Reverse proxies whose X-Forwarded-For may be trusted (otherwise the real client IP can be forged). X-Forwarded-For is believed only from these peers — otherwise the client IP can be forged (rate limit, lockout, fail2ban). IMPORTANT: start uvicorn **without** `--proxy-headers`. Otherwise uvicorn already replaces `request.client.host` with the forwarded IP and this check comes to nothing. |
| `redis_url` | `str` | `""` | e.g. redis://localhost:6379/0 |
| `trusted_redirect_hosts` | `list[str]` | `list` | Hosts that ?next= may point to absolutely (open-redirect protection; empty = relative paths only). The host of your own base_url always counts and need not be repeated here. |
| `security_log` | `str` | `""` | File the logger "tinysesam.security" additionally writes to — the feed for fail2ban (deploy/fail2ban/), e.g. /var/log/tinysesam/security.log. Empty = to the logger only; whoever sets up logging themselves leaves it empty. If the file is not writable, TinySesam warns and carries on. When NEWLY created it gets 0640 instead of the umask (also after a rotation), because it contains usernames and IP addresses; an already existing world-readable file is reported but not rewritten. If a THIRD user is to read along (log shipping, neither owner nor in the group), the way leads through the group: logrotate line `create 0640 tinysesam adm` (stands that way in deploy/fail2ban/tinysesam-jail.conf). Without it the file is created again at the next rotation with the group of the TinySesam process, and the shipping loses read access — not at the update, but only at the rotation. |
| `audit_retention_days` | `int` | `0` | Retention of the audit log in days: `auth.gc()` deletes older lines (B5-11). 0 = no deadline, the log grows without limit as before. The audit log contains usernames and IPs, i.e. personal data — a deadline is the operator's business (purpose and duration belong in their record of processing activities). The default therefore deletes nothing on its own. The command `tinysesam gc --audit-days N` does the same from the command line. Allowed are 0 to 3660 (ten years) — a value in seconds instead of days is rejected, not silently accepted. |
| `audit_ip_pseudonymize` | `bool` | `False` | Truncate IPs in the audit log to their network (IPv4 /24, IPv6 /48). Applies to new lines; lock, rate limit and security_log (fail2ban) still see the full address, otherwise a lock would hit the whole network. |
